meta.description: Genuinely Confucius: Analects 13.17, in James Legge's 1861 English. Big quote sites credit Wilson Mizner, an American playwright born in 1876.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Desire to have things done quickly prevents their being done thoroughly'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Confucius — Analects, Book XIII, ch. XVII, in James Legge's 1861 translation. Not Wilson Mizner, despite what the big quote databases say.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: c. 551 – c. 479 BC · Chinese philosopher and teacher
answer.sourceLine: This is a real passage of the Analects — Book XIII (Tsze-lu), chapter XVII — where Confucius answers his disciple Tsze-hsia, newly made governor of Chu-fu, on how to govern. The memorable English wording is James Legge’s, from The Chinese Classics, Vol. I (London: Trübner & Co., 1861), and it is printed there in full.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Analects, Book XIII (Tsze-lu), chapter XVII
Confucius, answering his disciple Tsze-hsia (Zi Xia), newly governor of Chu-fu
James Legge, in The Chinese Classics, Vol. I (London: Trübner & Co., 1861; reprinted 1893)

source.excerpt: Tsze-hsia, being governor of Chu-fu, asked about government. The Master said, “Do not be desirous to have things done quickly; do not look at small advantages. Desire to have things done quickly prevents their being done thoroughly. Looking at small advantages prevents great affairs from being accomplished.”
trail: Searching the exact wording leads straight to the Analects rather than to any modern speaker. Wikisource’s text of Legge’s Book XIII ↗ carries chapter XVII in full, including “Desire to have things done quickly prevents their being done thoroughly.”

Checked against the Chinese. The Chinese Text Project’s Zi Lu chapter, section 17 ↗ prints 子夏為莫父宰，問政 beside the same Legge English, so the sentence is a translation of 欲速，則不達 and not a floating aphorism.

Traced to the printed book. The Internet Archive’s scan ↗ gives the volume as The Chinese Classics … Vol. I. Confucian analects, the great learning, and the doctrine of the mean, James Legge, London: Trübner & Co., 1861; Wikisource describes its text ↗ as “A section of Vol. I of Legge’s Chinese Classics (1861), reprinted in 1893.”
Then the false trail. BrainyQuote ↗ and QuoteFancy ↗ both attribute the identical passage to Wilson Mizner, who was born in 1876 ↗ — after the wording was already in print.
source.excerptNote: Legge’s complete chapter XVII, as transcribed at Wikisource. The famous single sentence is the third of four; on its own it loses the fact that this was job advice to a specific new magistrate.

source.rightsNote: The Chinese original is more than two thousand years old and long out of copyright, and the English wording quoted here comes from James Legge’s translation first published in The Chinese Classics, Vol. I (London: Trübner & Co., 1861), with a second edition in 1893. Both printings are comfortably before 1931, so this specific translation is in the public domain in the United States — note that a modern rendering of the same passage by a living translator would not be.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.metaLine: c. 551 – c. 479 BC · Chinese philosopher, teacher and political adviser
author.bio: Confucius (Kụng Fūzạ) was a teacher and would-be statesman of the state of Lu who spent much of his life trying to persuade rulers to govern by moral example rather than coercion. He wrote no book of sayings himself: the Analects is a compilation of his remarks and conversations put together by disciples and later hands, and Wikipedia notes that these aphorisms were gathered “not until many years after his death.” The advice in this passage — don’t rush, don’t chase small gains — is characteristic of him: practical counsel given to a specific young official taking up a specific post.

The English wording "Desire to have things done quickly prevents their being done thoroughly" is Legge's. Quote sites that credit Wilson Mizner (1876–1933) are wrong: Legge printed the sentence in 1861.

misattribution.heading: Where it goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Confucius is sound — unusually so for a name this heavily counterfeited. What goes wrong with this quote is the opposite of the usual problem: two of the largest quote databases have taken a passage of the Analects and handed it to a 20th-century American wit.

items.scope: All four sentences of the passage
items.why: BrainyQuote ↗ and QuoteFancy ↗ both print the full Legge passage under Mizner’s name. Mizner was an American playwright and raconteur born in 1876 ↗; Legge’s English was already in print in the 1861 first edition of The Chinese Classics ↗. The dates alone settle it.

items.who: Confucius, as though he said it in these words
items.why: The thought is his; the sentence is his translator’s. Confucius’s reply in Chinese is four characters, 欲速不達. The polished English is James Legge’s 1861 rendering — a modern rendering of the same passage ↗ gives “Be neither hasty nor partial! For haste makes waste, and partiality loses entirety.”

Confucius wrote no collection of sayings. Wikipedia notes that his aphorisms “were compiled in the Analects, but not until many years after his death,” so every quotation from it is a report by disciples rather than an authored text. Confucius at Wikipedia ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Confucius said it, to a young magistrate named Tsze-hsia, in Book XIII, chapter XVII of the Analects ↗. The words you know it by are James Legge’s, published in 1861.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The advice was not a fridge magnet. Tsze-hsia (Zi Xia) had just been handed a town to run, and he asked his teacher what to do first. Confucius gave him two warnings rather than a programme: don’t rush, and don’t get distracted by small wins. In a system where a magistrate’s reputation was made or broken by visible results, both were counsel against the obvious career move.

The phrase became one of the most durable idioms in Chinese. A Taipei Times language column ↗ traces 欲速則不達 (yù sù zé bù dá) to this passage in the Zi Lu chapter, and notes it reappears in the Book of Han, completed in 111 AD, chapter 75. Its usual English equivalents are “more haste, less speed” and “haste makes waste.”
context.detailsSummary: How much of this sentence is Confucius, and how much is his translator?
detailsBody: Four Chinese characters carry the thought: 欲速不達 — roughly, want-fast, then not-arrive. Everything else in the famous English line is James Legge, a Victorian missionary-scholar working in Hong Kong, choosing a formal register that reads today like an aphorism carved into stone.

Other renderings look nothing like it. One modern version of 13.17 online ↗, which names no translator, compresses the whole exchange to “Be neither hasty nor partial! For haste makes waste, and partiality loses entirety.” Same passage, same meaning, entirely different sentence. That is why the specific string people search for belongs to Legge’s 1861 book even though the thought belongs to Confucius.
